entries.reason: He sank the trap again near midnight with heads for bait.
entries.text: Lifted the trap at the shallows: two crayfish in the inner cone and the bait heads picked down to shell. Six since I first sank it. Past the water a thin line of smoke was already leaning southwest out of the trees from that stone ring.
entries.title: Morning lift

entries.reason: Every boil costs lamp oil.
entries.text: Put the two in the tin with last night's one and set it over the bench lantern. One boil for three, as planned. The oil can sloshes lower every time I tip it; a little under a third now.
entries.title: One boil, three tails

entries.reason: He went to bed with nothing in him.
entries.text: Ate all three tails on the crate and cracked the claws for the bits. Not a meal, but my hands stopped shaking on the wrench.
entries.title: Breakfast

queries: how far does the sunset move along the horizon each day in november
entries.query: how far does the sunset move along the horizon each day in november
entries.reason: His first two sunset lines on the sheet landed on top of each other.
entries.source: EarthSky: Equinox fun: Track the sun's shift now until the solstice
entries.text: The sunset slides about half a degree a day at a middling latitude, one sun's width, fastest near the equinox and nearly stopped for two or three weeks around the solstice. Half a degree is a pencil width on my sheet, so two lines a night apart will always look like one. New rule: measure it in finger widths at arm's length off the compass's west, and draw a line only every fourth clear night.
entries.title: Half a degree

entries.reason: He peened the step sharp last night and wouldn't hop-test it in the dark.
entries.text: Hopped off the crate five times with the compass in my fist and the tail under the peened step. It held all five. There's a bright scratch on the step now where the tail rubs, so it will round off again; it's only a question of how many hops.
entries.title: Five hops

entries.reason: Three days in the current and the meal still dries his mouth, and he can't afford oil to boil it.
entries.text: Some trees just carry more bitter than others, even the same kind. One man found cold creek water slow or useless; another kneads the bag under running water, longer than you think. Kneading costs no oil, so that's what I'll try.
entries.title: Knead it longer

entries.reason: The tablet said to knead longer than you think.
entries.text: Knelt at the shallows and kneaded the net bag in the current with both hands, a hundred squeezes, and the water ran off it cloudy brown. Past the water a fresh gout of smoke went up thick from the stone ring, as if somebody just fed it. Tasted a pinch after: the dry edge is still there, a little less.
entries.title: Kneading

two metal parts rubbing wear how to reduce wear small catch harder steel or oil

entries.reason: The bright scratch on the peened step means the catch is already wearing.
entries.text: The first search only gave me house doors. The second: two of the same metal rubbing under load stick at the high spots and tear bits off each other, and grit in between grinds. A film of oil keeps them apart, and unlike metals don't weld, which is why gearmakers run steel on bronze.
entries.title: Weld and tear

entries.reason: Oil was the cheapest fix the tablet gave him.
entries.text: Wiped the step clean with my shirt tail and let one drop of lamp oil fall off the wick onto it, then worked the tail under it twenty times with the wrench. It slides instead of scraping now. One drop is nothing next to a boil, but the oil will catch grit, so it gets wiped every night.
entries.title: One drop

queries: what can you eat in the woods in november besides acorns
entries.query: what can you eat in the woods in november besides acorns
entries.reason: Down to crayfish tails, and the acorn meal isn't ready.
entries.source: Mother Earth News: Winter Foraging in New England
entries.text: Asked what else the woods give this late in the year: beechnuts, pine nuts, needle tea, wintergreen berries, willow catkins. I've paced a fair piece of this forest and seen oaks, ferns and fungus. None of that list grows here.
entries.title: Not this forest

queries: is it ok to eat acorn meal that is still a little bitter
entries.query: is it ok to eat acorn meal that is still a little bitter
entries.reason: Hungry enough to eat the meal before it's done, and wanted to know what that costs.
entries.source: Outdoors Codidact: Can I eat raw acorns?
entries.text: Unleached acorns eaten in quantity bind you up and may be hard on the kidneys, but the taste is so bad you'd quit before you ate enough to hurt. Mine is only dry at the edge. One small handful, and the rest stays in the current.
entries.title: Bitter is the warning

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped one small handful of meal into my palm, then sank it again. Past the water the smoke from the stone ring thickened and leaned southwest; somebody keeps that fire going all morning.
entries.title: One handful

entries.text: Ate the handful on the crate a pinch at a time. Gritty and dry at the back, nothing like bread, but it sits better than nothing. The bag gets kneaded again at dusk, before the trap lift.
entries.title: Gritty

queries: how to cook acorn meal into something without an oven or a fire
acorn mush just acorn meal and water how long to cook
entries.query: how to cook acorn meal into something without an oven or a fire
entries.reason: His meal is nearly leached and he can't keep eating it raw and gritty.
entries.source: Mother Earth News: Traditional Indigenous Acorn Mush
entries.text: The first search gave me bread and stew recipes that want ovens and beef. The second: one cup of meal to three of water, simmered about half an hour, or the old way, hot stones from a fire dropped right into the batter, and you peel the cooked chips off the stones after.
entries.title: Simmer or stones

entries.text: Half an hour of simmering on a lantern is a night's worth of oil. The stones want a fire, and the only fire around here is in that ring past the water, the one somebody keeps going all morning.
entries.title: No fire of mine

entries.text: Drew a small dotted circle on the sheet across the water from the stepping stones, where the smoke comes up, and wrote 'fire, kept all day' beside it. Dotted, because I haven't walked to it. The smoke is still leaning southwest.
entries.title: Dotted circle

entries.text: Dug through the scrap pile and came up with a flat square of thin sheet tin, a hand and a half wide, barely bent. It would do for a griddle to bake meal cakes on hot coals. I don't have hot coals.
entries.title: Square of tin

queries: acorn meal flat cakes cooked thin on hot metal how long
entries.query: acorn meal flat cakes cooked thin on hot metal how long
entries.reason: He had a square of tin for a griddle but no fire, and half an hour of simmering would drink his oil.
entries.source: The Inn at the Crossroads: Acorn Cakes
entries.text: An old recipe drops the batter by spoonfuls in a greased pan on low heat and cooks it half a minute a side, then looks underneath and flips it when it's lightly brown. Spoon-thin cooks in a minute or two, not half an hour. A minute of lantern I can pay for.
entries.title: Half a minute a side

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped out two handfuls, wet enough to be batter already. Sank the bag again under the stone.
entries.title: Two handfuls

entries.text: Patted the meal out thin on the tin square and held it over the bench lantern with the flame turned up. No grease, so it stuck; the edges browned and lifted in about two minutes, but I had to scrape the middle loose with the wrench to flip it, and it tore. Four minutes of flame, all told.
entries.title: Stuck

entries.text: Ate both halves on the crate. Crisp at the edges, gummy in the middle, and the dry bitter edge mostly hides under the toast. Next one thinner, and the tin wants something greasy I don't have.
entries.title: Better hot

queries: how to grease a pan with no oil or butter camping
can you get oil out of acorns
entries.query: how to grease a pan with no oil or butter camping
entries.reason: The first cake stuck to the dry tin and tore, and he has nothing greasy in camp.
entries.source: Living Wild: Pressing Acorns into Oil
entries.text: Every answer to the first wants shortening, bacon fat or paper to line the pan: kitchen things. Acorns do hold oil, some kinds nearly a third, but you get it out with a hand press and an afternoon, and the two men who tried got it wrong the first time. No press, no fat. The tin goes dry, so the cake has to change instead.
entries.title: Nothing greasy

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped one handful of meal, half what I took last time, and sank the bag again. Thinner this time.
entries.title: Half as much

entries.text: Held the tin over the lantern until a drop of water off my finger skittered across it, then pressed the meal on as thin as a fingernail and kept my hands off. The edges lifted on their own, and it came up under the wrench in one piece, one corner left behind.
entries.title: Hot tin first

entries.onMind: how many cakes the bag has left in it
entries.text: Ate the thin one on the crate: crisp all through, almost a cracker, and the bitter barely there. Past the water the smoke from the stone ring went up thick again, like somebody just fed it.
entries.title: Almost a cracker

queries: how many hours does a hurricane lantern burn on a quart of oil
entries.query: how many hours does a hurricane lantern burn on a quart of oil
entries.reason: Every cake and every boil comes out of the oil can, and he has never worked out how long what's left will actually last.
entries.text: A big storm lantern holding about a quart is rated for a day and a night of burning at an ordinary flame, and turned high it burns faster, smokes and blackens the globe. Outdoors you keep the wick lower because wind makes it smoke. I have under a third of a quart: eight or nine hours of one flame, all told, and three lanterns at dusk would drink that in three nights.
entries.title: A day and a night

entries.onMind: Eight or nine hours of flame left, and every cake costs some of it.
entries.text: The bench lantern's globe is black down one side from cooking with the flame up. Wound the wick down with the wrench until it went out. One lantern tonight, low, and the other two stay dark.
entries.title: Turned down

entries.text: Picked up thirty-one acorns under the oak on the east bank. Twelve have a neat round hole in the shell the size of a pencil point, and the one I split had a fat white grub curled inside. Kept nineteen.
entries.title: Grub holes

entries.text: Hammered the nineteen open on the bench with the wrench. Two were brown and powdery inside, so seventeen good meats went into the dented tin. They go in a second bag in the current once I have cord for one.
entries.title: Seventeen good

queries: can you eat the grubs inside acorns
entries.query: can you eat the grubs inside acorns
entries.reason: Twelve of the acorns had holes, one had a fat white grub in it, and he's eating crumbs.
entries.source: Eat The Weeds: Acorn Grubs: Bait, Trailside Nibble
entries.text: Acorn grubs are eaten: raw they're mild and a bit chewy, like a piece of fat, and cooked they go soft and buttery, but in hot fat they burst in about a second. The grubs leave the acorn and drop to the ground, so that neat round hole is the way out; most of my twelve will be empty.
entries.title: Like a piece of fat

entries.text: Hammered the twelve holed shells open on the bench. Nine were empty except for brown dust; three still had a grub curled in them, fat in the middle, no legs.
entries.title: Nine doors out

entries.onMind: the trap lift at dusk, and the sunset before that
entries.text: Ate the three raw on the crate. Mild, chewy like a rind of fat, a little acorn at the end. Three is a mouthful, not a meal.
entries.title: Rind of fat

entries.text: Split the gray stalks with my thumbnail and twisted the fibers into cord at the stand, reversing every twist so it locks. One arm's length so far; a bag for seventeen meats wants four.
entries.title: One arm's length

queries: can you eat leached acorn meal raw without cooking it
entries.query: can you eat leached acorn meal raw without cooking it
entries.reason: Nearly empty and rationing oil, he wanted to know if the meal could be eaten without the lantern.
entries.source: Codidact Outdoors: Can I eat raw acorns?
entries.text: Nothing on the page says acorn meal has to be cooked. It's the bitter that does the harm, binds you up and is hard on the kidneys, and leaching is what takes it out: crack, soak, change the water, grind. So raw is fine once it's sweet. Mine still has a dry edge, so small handfuls, and no oil spent on a griddle tonight.
entries.title: Leached is enough

queries: what else can you burn in a hurricane lantern besides lamp oil
entries.query: what else can you burn in a hurricane lantern besides lamp oil
entries.reason: He read this afternoon that his oil is eight or nine hours of flame, and acorns hold oil.
entries.source: Outdoor Life: Survival Gear: Which Fuels to Use and Which to Avoid for Oil Lamps
entries.text: Clear lamp oil or clear kerosene, and that's the list. Thick oil has a high flash point and climbs the wick too slowly, so it burns dim and fitful and ruins the wick, and the light stuff that would climb fast is the kind that blows up. Acorn oil would be the thick kind, even if I had a press. The third of a quart is all the light there is.
entries.title: Only the thin stuff

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped a small handful into my palm. Still the dry edge at the back, so small it stays; the bag goes back under the stone for another day of current.
entries.title: A small handful

entries.onMind: what the small one is cooking
entries.text: The stone ring is lit again, and from the edge of the brambles it smells like toast. The small one is crouched at it holding a stick out over the coals. Cooking. I went north around the brambles, wide of it.
entries.title: Toast

entries.text: Ate the meal a pinch at a time with my back to the trees while the sun went in a hand left of west again. Not a line night; I only draw every fourth.
entries.title: Third clear night

entries.text: Whatever crouches at that fire is roasting acorns, same as me, and it has a fire all day where I have a third of a quart. Back home they'd say keep away from what you don't understand. Back home they said there was no west.
entries.title: Keep away

entries.onMind: one lantern, a third of a quart
entries.text: Walked back east in the last of the light and lit only the bench lantern, the wick wound down with the wrench to a sliver. Across the water the stone ring is still glowing orange between the trunks.
entries.title: A sliver of flame

entries.text: Wiped the peened step and held the tail up to the lantern. The bright scratch is no longer than this morning; since the drop of oil it slides in and clicks.
entries.title: Nightly wipe

entries.text: Twisted the split fibers on the crate, reversing every twist so it locks. Two arm's lengths now, half a bag's worth.
entries.title: Two arm's lengths

entries.text: Hung my whole weight off the left side-spar joint, twice. It creaked each time and gave nothing, and there's no wind tonight to rattle it. The frapping holds dead weight; a gust is another question.
entries.title: Dead weight

entries.text: Left the lantern on the bench and went down to the shallows in the dark. Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped two handfuls by feel; the stone ring across the water gave just enough light to find the edge of the bag.
entries.title: By the other fire

entries.onMind: the small one by the fire
entries.text: The small one is sitting on the log by that fire now, a dark round head against the glow, hardly moving. It never looked my way.
entries.title: Sitting still

entries.text: Felt along the trap in the cold water: the funnel mouth was packed with wet oak leaves, a fistful, and nothing inside. With the leaves coming down like this, that door will clog every night.
entries.title: Leaves in the door

entries.onMind: a leaf hood for the trap
entries.text: Picked the mouth clean by feel. It wants a hood over the door, stalks laid pointing downstream so leaves slide off and a crayfish still walks under. Daylight job.
entries.title: A hood

entries.text: Ate both handfuls raw on the crate by the low bench lantern, wet, with the dry edge at the back. The tin square stays cold tonight; that's the deal I made with the oil can.
entries.title: Two cold handfuls

entries.text: Twisted split fibers on the crate by the low lantern, reversing every twist. Three arm's lengths now; one more is a bag's worth.
entries.title: Three arm's lengths

entries.reason: The trap door wants a hood of stalks laid pointing downstream.
entries.text: Left the lantern on the bench and snapped long gray stalks off the stand by feel. Across the water the small one was bent over a flat stone by its fire, picking things up one at a time and dropping them in a sack.
entries.title: Stalks by feel

entries.text: Laid the stalks out on the plank bench and sorted them long from short. Fourteen long straight ones, enough for a hood if I lay them close. The lashing waits for daylight.
entries.title: Fourteen straight

entries.onMind: laying the hood on the trap at first light
entries.text: It was picking its acorns up off that stone before the night wet got them. I never thought about dew; mine are all in the current anyway.
entries.title: Before the wet

entries.text: Four arm's lengths of stalk cord by the lantern sliver, every twist reversed so it locks. That's a bag's worth if I knot it tight.
entries.title: Four arm's lengths

entries.reason: The next batch of acorns needs a bag of its own in the current.
entries.text: Cut a gauge stick two fingers wide off a short stalk and started the net around it, a sheet bend at every mesh. Three rows by the sliver of light; my thumbs are going numb.
entries.title: First rows

entries.onMind: something to line the second net
entries.text: Two fingers is fine for whole meats but crushed meal would wash straight through it. It gets a cloth lining like the first, if I can find cloth.
entries.title: Too wide for crumbs

entries.text: Two hours after I picked it clean, a thin layer of leaves in the mouth again, and behind it one crayfish walking the inner cone. It goes in the dented tin for breakfast.
entries.title: One under the leaves

entries.text: Across the water the small one sat on the log by its fire with its round head tipped back, looking straight up, still as a stone. The low owl did its five from upstream and nothing answered.
entries.title: Head tipped back

entries.text: Scooped two handfuls off the net bag by the other fire's light and ate one squatting in the cold water. The dry edge is fainter tonight; another day of current.
entries.title: Dry edge fainter

entries.text: Squatting at the bag, I saw the small one come down to the still pool across from me and kneel to drink. I sloshed twice getting my feet out of the cold, and its round head came up and turned my way. I stayed still as a post until it went back to its fire.
entries.title: It looked over

entries.text: Ate the second handful of wet meal on the crate. Still a little dry at the back of the tongue, and it doesn't fill the hole.
entries.title: Second handful

entries.text: From the bench I watched the glow across the water go down to nothing; the small one put its fire to bed early. Mine's the only light now, and it's a sliver.
entries.title: Its fire went dark

entries.text: Six rows on the gauge stick. Every other knot I stop and blow on my thumbs; the bench is wet with dew.
entries.title: Six rows

entries.text: Seventh and eighth rows. Counting meshes out loud keeps the sheet bends even: eleven across, and the bag is about a hand deep now.
entries.title: Eleven across

entries.text: Drank four handfuls from the shallows to fill the gap the meal left. Across the water it is all dark now, no glow and no small one, only the pool showing a few stars.
entries.title: Water for supper

entries.text: A wet wad of leaves in the mouth again and nothing behind it. Picked it clean by feel and sank it back under the stone.
entries.title: Only leaves

entries.onMind: lashing the hood at first light
entries.text: The trap fills with leaves about as fast as the trees drop them. Either the hood sends them over the top, or I'm feeding the creek's whole autumn through a door one thumb wide.
entries.title: The whole autumn

entries.text: Three more arm's lengths of stalk cord on the crate, twisted tight and doubled back on itself. That's enough to lash a hood and some left over.
entries.title: Enough cord

entries.text: Couldn't wait for first light. Lashed the long stalks into a crooked hood frame on the bench by feel, every crossing tied twice. It goes over the trap mouth at first light, and either the leaves ride over it or I've built them a roof.
entries.title: A hood frame

entries.onMind: re-lashing the right joint in daylight
entries.text: Hung my weight off the right side-spar joint, same as the left. The frapping slid a finger's width with a crack of cord and the spar dropped. Nothing broke, but that joint is loose now and I said a few things to it.
entries.title: Right joint slipped

entries.text: Wiped the compass step; the scratch hasn't grown. The left joint I lashed in daylight and it held. The right one I did by a sliver of lantern, and it didn't. Daylight work stays daylight work.
entries.title: Tied in the dark
